claims.text: In refractory high-entropy alloys, retention of toughness is governed by nanoprecipitate presence, coherency, size, and distribution.
Coherent nanoprecipitates promote plastic deformation by permitting dislocation transmission across phase boundaries.
Dislocation transmission through coherent interfaces prevents excessive local stress accumulation and premature crack initiation.
Thermal coarsening or loss of precipitate coherency causes toughness loss.
The initial refractory HEA contains SCCP-produced fine, coherent δ-lamellae with embedded γ″ particles.
A controlled aging treatment can vary precipitate size, coherency, and distribution.
The proposed behavior applies from ambient to moderately elevated tensile-testing temperatures while the designed phases remain stable.
The δ-lamellae and γ″ particles, together with their coherence to the matrix, are the relevant structural mediator.
Dislocations shear through the coherent δ-lamellae and cross coherent δ/γ interfaces during deformation.
Shearing of coherent δ-lamellae accommodates large local deformation rather than creating a crack, alleviating local stress concentration.
Coarsened or incoherent precipitates act as stress concentrators that promote crack nucleation and propagation.
Specimens with optimally refined, coherent precipitates will absorb more energy before fracture than specimens with coarsened or incoherent precipitates.
Specimens with optimally refined, coherent precipitates will have greater tensile ductility than specimens with coarsened or incoherent precipitates.
The baseline is the as-processed SCCP refractory HEA with fine, coherent nanoprecipitates.
The hypothesis generalizes to refractory HEAs, including W-based HEAs processed by SCCPs, provided phase stability is maintained.
Extensive oxidation or phase transformations outside the designed operating window can invalidate the proposed behavior.
TEM and STEM measurements combined with mechanical tests can correlate precipitate characteristics and dislocation behavior with toughness.

The hypothesis is falsified if heat-treatment-induced changes in precipitate size or coherency produce no statistically significant toughness difference, particularly if coarsened or incoherent specimens are not less tough than the baseline.
